paragraphs: So far we have considered the prince as a moral and collective person, unified by the force of the laws and holding the executive power in the State. We now have to consider this power when it is gathered into the hands of a natural person, a real man, who alone has the right to dispose of it in accordance with the laws. Such a person is called a monarch or king.

Unlike the other forms of administration, in which a collective being stands for an individual, in this form an individual stands for a collective being. The moral unity that constituted the prince is therefore at the same time a physical unity, and all the qualities that in the other case the law brings together only with difficulty are found naturally united.

Thus the will of the people, the will of the prince, the public force of the State and the particular force of the government all answer to a single motive power. All the springs of the machine are in the same hands, and the whole moves toward the same end. There are no conflicting movements to cancel one another, and no kind of constitution can be imagined in which less effort produces more action. Archimedes, sitting quietly on the shore and easily drawing a great ship afloat, stands in my mind for a skillful monarch, governing vast states from his study and moving everything while he seems himself unmoved.

But if no government is more vigorous than this one, there is also none in which the particular will holds more sway and rules the rest more easily. Everything moves toward the same end, indeed, but this end is by no means the public happiness, and even the force of the administration constantly proves harmful to the State.

Kings want to be absolute, and men are always crying out to them from afar that the best means of being so is to get themselves loved by their people. This precept is all very well, and even in some respects very true. Unfortunately, it will always be laughed at in courts. The power that comes from a people’s love is no doubt the greatest, but it is precarious and conditional, and princes will never be content with it. The best kings want to be in a position to be wicked, if they please, without losing their mastery. Political preachers may tell them to their hearts’ content that, since the people’s strength is their own, their first interest is that the people should be prosperous, numerous and formidable; kings know very well that this is untrue. Their first personal interest is that the people should be weak, wretched and unable to resist them. I admit that if the subjects always remained submissive, the prince’s interest would indeed be for the people to be powerful, so that its power, being his own, might make him formidable to his neighbors. But this interest is only secondary and subordinate, and strength is incompatible with submission, so princes naturally always prefer the principle that serves their immediate advantage. This is what Samuel put forcefully to the Hebrews, and what Machiavelli has clearly shown. He professed to teach kings, but it was the people he really taught. His _Prince_ is the book of Republicans.[1]

We found, on general grounds, that monarchy suits only great States, and this is confirmed when we examine it in itself. The more numerous the public administration, the smaller the relation between the prince and the subjects becomes, and the nearer it comes to equality, so that in democracy the ratio is unity, or absolute equality. Conversely, as the government is restricted in numbers the ratio increases, and it reaches its _maximum_ when the government is in the hands of one person. There is then too great a distance between prince and people, and the State lacks a bond of union. To form such a bond there must be intermediate orders, and princes, personages and nobility to make them up. But none of this suits a small State, to which all class differences mean ruin.

If, however, it is hard for a great State to be well governed, it is much harder for it to be well governed by a single man; and everyone knows what happens when kings appoint others to take their place.

An essential and inevitable defect, which will always rank monarchical government below republican, is that in a republic the public voice hardly ever raises to the highest positions anyone who is not enlightened and capable, and who does not do them honor. In monarchies, by contrast, those who rise to the top are most often merely petty blunderers, petty swindlers and petty intriguers, whose petty talents get them into the highest positions at Court but, as soon as they have arrived, serve only to make their ineptitude clear to the public. The people is far less often mistaken in its choice than the prince, and a man of real worth among the king’s ministers is almost as rare as a fool at the head of a republican government. Thus, when by some fortunate chance one of these born governors takes the helm of State in a monarchy that has been nearly overwhelmed by swarms of “gentlemanly” administrators, there is nothing but amazement at the resources he discovers, and his coming marks an era in his country’s history.

For a monarchical State to have a chance of being well governed, its population and extent must be proportionate to the abilities of its governor. It is easier to conquer than to rule. With a long enough lever, the world could be moved with one finger; to sustain it takes the shoulders of Hercules. However small a State may be, the prince is hardly ever big enough for it. When, on the other hand, the State happens to be too small for its ruler — which is rare — it is also ill governed, because the ruler, constantly pursuing his great designs, forgets the interests of the people, and makes it no less wretched by misusing the talents he has than a ruler of less capacity would make it for want of those he lacks. A kingdom should, so to speak, expand or contract with each reign, according to the prince’s capabilities. But the abilities of a senate are more constant in quantity, so the State can then have permanent frontiers without the administration suffering.

The disadvantage most felt in monarchical government is the lack of the continuous succession which, in both the other forms, provides an unbroken bond of union. When one king dies, another is needed. Elections leave dangerous intervals and are full of storms; and unless the citizens are disinterested and upright to a degree that very seldom goes with this kind of government, intrigue and corruption abound. He to whom the State has sold itself can hardly help selling it in his turn, and repaying himself, at the expense of the weak, the money the powerful have wrung from him. Under such an administration, venality sooner or later spreads through every part, and the peace enjoyed under a king is worse than the disorders of an interregnum.

What has been done to prevent these evils? Crowns have been made hereditary in certain families, and an order of succession has been set up, to prevent disputes from arising on the death of kings. That is to say, the disadvantages of regency have been put in place of those of election, apparent tranquillity has been preferred to wise administration, and men have chosen to risk having children, monsters or imbeciles as rulers rather than have disputes over the choice of good kings. It has not been taken into account that, in exposing ourselves to the risks this possibility entails, we are setting almost all the chances against us. There was sound sense in what the younger Dionysius said to his father, who reproached him for some shameful deed by asking, “Did I set you the example?” “No,” answered his son, “but your father was not king.”
